historical_timeline.summary: Begins service in the U.S. Senate.
Seeks medical advice for blood in the urine; not treated.
Several small benign bladder growths found and removed.
Possibly cancerous bladder tissue treated with thiotepa and five weeks of X-ray therapy.
Radical cystectomy with removal of the prostate and a small-intestine urinary conduit at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center.
Inoperable pelvic recurrence found at an operation for bowel obstruction.

claims.statement: Hubert Horatio Humphrey Jr. was born on 27 May 1911 in Wallace, South Dakota.
Humphrey served in the U.S. Senate from Minnesota from 1949 to 1964, as vice president from 1965 to 1969, and again in the Senate from 1971 until his death.

Humphrey sought medical advice in 1967 for blood in his urine; some doctors suspected bladder cancer, others disagreed, and he was not treated. In 1968 doctors found and removed several pinhead-size nonmalignant growths from his bladder. In 1994 researchers reported a p53 gene mutation in bladder cells from a 1967 urine sample of his.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Hematuria with benign bladder growths years before the diagnosis of cancer; the 1994 report is a retrospective molecular study.

source_links.locator: Title-level record of the 1994 report; the article was not read

claims.statement: In 1973 doctors found possibly cancerous tissue in his bladder and treated it with thiotepa and X-ray therapy, given five minutes a day for five weeks.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Intravesical chemotherapy and pelvic radiation for suspected early bladder cancer.

claims.statement: After three years free of cancer, an examination at the National Naval Medical Center in Bethesda for symptoms of a urinary tract infection found a low-grade malignancy, and in October 1976 a six-hour radical cystectomy at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center removed his bladder, prostate, lymph nodes, the fatty tissue around the bladder, and part of the urethra; the ureters were joined to a conduit made from a segment of small intestine, brought out to an opening on the skin to the right of the navel and drained into a bag. The nodes were to be examined for spread, and an experimental two-drug chemotherapy might be offered.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Radical cystoprostatectomy with an ileal conduit urinary diversion. The nodal result and any treatment after the operation were not reported in the fetched sources.

claims.statement: He resumed his Senate duties in January 1977, serving as deputy president pro tempore from January 5, 1977.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Used only to place his return to full-time work.

source_links.locator: Infobox and later Senate career section

claims.statement: In August 1977 doctors found a malignant tumor on his pelvic bone during a four-hour operation in Minneapolis to relieve a bowel obstruction; the cancer was described as inoperable and terminal, and chemotherapy was planned. He returned to the Senate eleven weeks later, with further chemotherapy scheduled.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Pelvic recurrence ten months after cystectomy. It falls after the synthetic episode and is used only as history.

claims.statement: Humphrey died on 13 January 1978 in Waverly, Minnesota.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as a fact; no detail of his last months is used.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care after radical cystoprostatectomy with an ileal conduit for urothelial bladder cancer, on the AUA/ASCO/SUO muscle-invasive bladder cancer guideline, the AUA/SUO non-muscle-invasive guideline, and the CMID urologic cancer monograph: how high-risk non-muscle-invasive disease that recurs after intravesical therapy and earlier pelvic radiation leads to early cystectomy, and how often the final pathology is upstaged; why pT2a N0 disease needs no adjuvant therapy; surveillance by cross-sectional imaging every 6 to 12 months and upper-tract and kidney function checks every 6 months; the metabolic effects of an ileal conduit (hyperchloremic acidosis, kidney function, vitamin B12); stoma and peristomal skin care; and the difference between expected bacteriuria in conduit urine and a true kidney infection, with a culture taken by catheter from the stoma. His documented history of bladder growths, intravesical thiotepa with X-ray therapy, and a radical cystectomy with a small-intestine conduit frames the episode.

documentation.chief_complaint: Four-week follow-up after cystectomy; appliance leaks and sore skin around the stoma; urology seen today

hpi.narrative: Mr. Humphrey returns four weeks after his first visit, four months after his radical cystoprostatectomy. For three weeks his appliance has leaked about twice a week, usually at night, and the skin under the lower edge of the wafer has become red and sore. He has had no fever, flank pain, or blood in the urine. He saw Dr. Kowalczyk of urology this morning with the wound, ostomy, and continence nurse, who measured the stoma and fitted a convex wafer with a barrier ring, stoma powder for the irritated skin, and a night drainage bag. Dr. Kowalczyk reviewed the pathology and agreed that he needs no further treatment, and set out the surveillance schedule. Erections have not returned since the operation; he understands why and does not want treatment now. He is back at full-time work, walks 20 to 30 minutes a day, and his appetite is good.

referral.question: Man of 65, three months after radical cystoprostatectomy with an ileal conduit at a cancer center for multifocal urothelial carcinoma with carcinoma in situ, pT2a N0, margins negative. Please share his survivorship surveillance close to home, review his stoma, and set the metabolic monitoring plan
referral.pertinent_history: Blood in the urine decades ago; small benign bladder growths removed; later, possibly cancerous tissue treated with intravesical thiotepa and five weeks of pelvic radiation. After three years free of disease, cystoscopy for urinary symptoms found recurrent multifocal low-grade papillary tumors with high-grade carcinoma in situ in a small, radiation-affected bladder, and he had an early radical cystoprostatectomy with pelvic node dissection, partial urethrectomy, and an ileal conduit. Final pathology: high-grade urothelial carcinoma invading the inner half of the muscularis propria (pT2a), 0 of 18 nodes, ureteric and urethral margins negative, prostate without urothelial involvement. Pre-operative CT showed no spread. No chemotherapy was given before or after surgery. Recovery uncomplicated; back at full-time work. Creatinine 1.12 mg/dL (eGFR 73), chloride 106, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, vitamin B12 412 pg/mL. PHQ-9 score 3. Appliance leaks at night have started in the past week. No regular medicines. Tobacco history not recorded
questions: Is any adjuvant treatment indicated for pT2a N0 disease with negative margins?
What surveillance imaging and tests does he need, at what intervals, and which should primary care arrange?
How should his appliance leaks and peristomal skin be managed, and which stoma complications should we watch for?
What kidney and metabolic monitoring does the ileal conduit need (creatinine, acid-base, vitamin B12), and when should we treat?
How should we interpret urine findings with a conduit, and when should infection be treated?
Does the remaining urethra need surveillance?

assessment.display: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder, pT2a pN0, margins negative, after radical cystoprostatectomy
assessment.assessment: Organ-confined, node-negative disease. Upstaging from non-muscle-invasive disease at resection to pT2a at cystectomy is common, which is one reason early cystectomy is offered for high-risk disease that recurs after intravesical therapy, especially in an irradiated bladder. Adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy or immunotherapy is offered for pT3 to pT4 or node-positive disease; for pT2a N0 with negative margins, the benefit does not justify the toxicity, and none is recommended. The main risks are recurrence in the pelvis or at distant sites and a new tumor in the upper tracts or the urethra

assessment.display: Ileal conduit urostomy with appliance leaks and moisture dermatitis
assessment.assessment: The leaks come from a skin crease below the stoma when he sits, which a flat wafer cannot seal. The skin change is irritant dermatitis from urine, not candida. The stoma itself is healthy, with good spout height. Later problems to watch for are parastomal hernia, stomal stenosis or retraction, and peristomal skin overgrowth from chronic urine contact

assessment.display: Kidney and metabolic effects of the ileal conduit
assessment.assessment: Reabsorption of chloride and ammonium from urine in the ileal segment causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis in some patients; his bicarbonate is at the lower limit. Kidney function can decline from infection, obstruction at the ureteric anastomoses, or reflux. Vitamin B12 deficiency is uncommon with the short segment used for a conduit, but yearly checks are advised from two to three years after surgery

Conduit urine is almost always colonized, and the dipstick and culture from the bag are usually abnormal. Bacteriuria without symptoms should not be treated. Fever, flank pain, rigors, or a rise in creatinine suggest upper-tract infection, which needs a culture taken by sterile catheter through the stoma and prompt treatment

The urethral margin was negative and the prostatic urethra was not involved, so the risk of urethral recurrence is low and routine urethral wash cytology is not needed; bloody discharge from the urethra should be reported

recommendations: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with a urographic phase at one year after surgery, then every 6 to 12 months to three years, then yearly; urology review with each scan
